Financial planning · Disability savings · Visual planning guide

An RDSP withdrawal has two outflows: the beneficiary payment and the grant repayment

Four graphics explain an ordinary proportional repayment, the remaining assistance holdback and the difference between cash requested, cash paid and value removed from the plan.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Separate an RDSP payment from the government repayment

Separate grant/bond repayment$15,000
Requested payment not illustrated$0

Ordinary proportional-repayment illustration only: beneficiary remains DTC-eligible, is under 60, and the issuer has independently confirmed the AHA and remaining annual payment capacity. It does not determine DAP/LDAP entitlement, annual statutory limits, tax composition or net cash after tax. Requested cash is capped at the entered annual capacity and plan value above the confirmed AHA. The government repayment is the lesser of three times that gross payment and the entered AHA, reducing both plan value and the AHA. No new grants, withdrawals, returns or passage of time are assumed. AHA above plan value produces no payment here and requires issuer review. DTC loss, SDSP/specified-year exceptions, closure and death require different treatment.

The central idea

A gross payment to the beneficiary can trigger a separate government repayment. Check both outflows and the issuer’s payment capacity before treating an account balance as available cash.

01

Start with a confirmed payment type and holdback snapshot

An RDSP supports long-term saving for a person with a disability. A spending decision needs more than an account value: the issuer must establish the payment rules, the assistance holdback amount and any annual payment capacity that applies.

The CRA’s payment guide distinguishes disability assistance payments from lifetime disability assistance payments, and explains that payment limits depend on the plan’s situation. An entered capacity in this tool means a remaining amount already confirmed by the issuer. The calculator does not establish that capacity itself.

This example isolates an ordinary proportional-repayment case: a beneficiary under 60 with continuing Disability Tax Credit eligibility. It excludes specified disability savings plans, specified-year exceptions, DTC-loss cases, closure and death. Those situations can require different treatment. A result here cannot substitute for the issuer’s assessment of a real request.

02

Trace a CAD 5,000 request through both outflows

The hypothetical plan starts at CAD 100,000. Its confirmed assistance holdback amount is CAD 21,000, and independently confirmed remaining annual payment capacity is CAD 10,000. The beneficiary requests a gross payment of CAD 5,000.

For the ordinary case, the CRA’s RDSP guide describes a proportional repayment of CAD 3 of grants and bonds for each CAD 1 withdrawn, capped at the assistance holdback amount. The example therefore repays min(3 × 5,000, 21,000) = CAD 15,000.

Two outflows reduce the account: CAD 5,000 for the beneficiary and CAD 15,000 for the government. Remaining plan value is 100,000 − 5,000 − 15,000 = CAD 80,000. The government repayment is additional to the gross beneficiary payment. It is not taken a second time from that CAD 5,000.

The payment may contain taxable amounts. This illustration does not calculate that composition, tax payable, benefit interactions or the beneficiary’s after-tax spending money. “Gross beneficiary payment” is deliberately the label used in the charts.

03

Read the bend where the holdback cap is reached

The curve compares independent payment alternatives from the same opening snapshot. With a CAD 21,000 holdback, the three-to-one repayment reaches its cap at a CAD 7,000 gross payment.

Below that point, an extra CAD 1 of payment increases total plan depletion by CAD 4 in this narrow example: CAD 1 to the beneficiary and CAD 3 repaid. Above the cap, the repayment remains CAD 21,000. A CAD 10,000 permitted payment would therefore remove CAD 31,000 in total.

This is arithmetic for one event under the stated conditions. It does not describe investment performance, an annual expense ratio or a tax rate. Nor is the curve a series of withdrawals: every point starts with the same original assets and holdback.

The formula matrix keeps this distinction visible. Each cell shows only the capped repayment formula. A displayed number does not confirm that its hypothetical withdrawal satisfies annual limits or leaves adequate assets.

04

Keep the remaining restriction separate from remaining assets

After the default event, repaying CAD 15,000 also reduces the entered holdback from CAD 21,000 to CAD 6,000. The second comparison chart shows that amount alongside CAD 80,000 of remaining assets.

The two quantities must not be added. Holdback identifies a repayment-related amount within the plan’s circumstances; it is not another investment account. ESDC’s technical guidance explains that the applicable period and repayment obligation depend on the event, age and DTC status, and that earlier repayments must be considered.

The calculator conservatively caps the beneficiary payment at both the entered annual capacity and plan value above the confirmed opening holdback. It then applies the separate repayment. If the entered holdback already exceeds plan value, the tool illustrates no payment and leaves the discrepancy for issuer review.

For example, with CAD 25,000 of assets and CAD 21,000 of holdback, only CAD 4,000 lies above that opening restriction. Even an entered annual capacity of CAD 10,000 does not make the full request fundable in this illustration.

05

Use the actual assistance history before making a date decision

A recent contribution date, a recent grant date and an account-opening date are different facts. The assistance calculation needs the issuer’s grant, bond and repayment history and the applicable event rules. A blanket instruction to wait ten years from the latest personal deposit can answer the wrong question.

This tool accepts a confirmed holdback snapshot. It does not age individual grants, reconstruct past repayments, predict new grants or roll a future date forward. Lowering the holdback control means testing another assumed snapshot; it does not establish that the lower number will apply on a chosen date.

  1. Confirm the payment type and gross amount with the issuer.
  2. Obtain the assistance holdback and remaining annual capacity for the actual request.
  3. Separate beneficiary cash, government repayment and remaining assets.
  4. Check the payment’s tax composition and any benefit interactions separately.
  5. Place the confirmed spendable amount in the household’s spending calendar.

The purpose is to understand the two outflows before committing the money. It does not recommend a withdrawal, determine program eligibility or calculate a personalized disability-savings strategy.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Charts labelled “Official statistics” or “Derived from official statistics” identify their source periods. Other charts are hypothetical scenarios. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. CRA · Take money out of an RDSP ↗

    Live official HTML reviewed 25 October 2026. Supports the distinction between payment types, differing annual rules, holdback-related payment constraints and taxable payment components. The tool takes an issuer-confirmed capacity and does not calculate an annual statutory limit.

  2. CRA · Registered Disability Savings Plan guide: proportional repayment ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026 for the ordinary three-to-one repayment capped at AHA. Exceptions and other triggering events require separate review. All account values and payment examples are hypothetical.

  3. ESDC · Assistance holdback amount and repayment obligation ↗

    Official issuer guidance reviewed 25 October 2026. Provides event/status/age distinctions and the need to account for prior repayments. No private history, future grant schedule or actual entitlement is reconstructed.
